source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Appending 'Wait' to stretch thinking first helps then hurts. At a fixed 16K-token budget, N short parallel chains with majority vote beat one stretched chain. They explain it by output variance rising with thinking length.
numbers: Fig 2a: accuracy 82.2% to 87.3% as mean thinking tokens go 385 to 1100, then falls to 70.3% at 15,980 tokens. Fig 8: at 16K budget, parallel thinking is about 22% above 'Wait & Think More' and about 47% above 'Exact Thinking'. Abstract says up to 20% over extended thinking. Models: R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B, Llama-8B. Data: GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024.
quote: parallel thinking yields up to 22% higher accuracy compared to sequential scaling
limits: Only small distilled models (authors say mid-sized only). Sequential arm is forced 'Wait' appending, not the model's own budget control or s1-style training. Majority vote needs a checkable single answer. No split by item difficulty. No verifier cost (vote only).
agent_relevance: Supports capping a single chain and spending leftover budget on several short chains for checkable answers on small models. Does not settle frontier models.

source: Sharma and Chopra (2025) The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute
finding: Direct counter to d01. At matched token budget, sequential refinement (each chain sees earlier attempts) beat parallel independent chains in 43 of 45 configurations on 5 open instruct models and 3 benchmarks.
numbers: 43/45 = 95.6% wins. Largest gap: Qwen3-235B-Instruct-2507, AIME-2025, 6 chains: 76.7% vs 30.0% (46.7 points). Each chain capped at 4096 tokens; 6 chains = 24,576 tokens in both arms. Budget sweep 2K to 16K tokens. Accuracy steps of 3.33 points on AIME imply about 30 problems per cell. Inverse-entropy weighting adds only +0.5 to +3.4 over majority vote in the parallel setting.
quote: sequential scaling where chains explicitly build upon previous attempts consistently outperforms the dominant parallel self-consistency paradigm in 95.6% of configurations
limits: Sequential here means iterative refinement with instruct (non-thinking) models, not budget forcing in one thinking trace, so it is not the same contrast as d01. A 4096-token cap per independent chain probably truncates parallel chains on AIME (my inference). Small n (about 30 per AIME cell), seed 42, temperature 0.7, no confidence intervals. Math and GPQA only. Authors list serial latency as a cost. Preprint, no peer review seen.
agent_relevance: Result flips with the definition of sequential and the chain cap. For our scaffold: revision with feedback can beat resampling at equal tokens when chains are short, so test both arms; do not trust either camp alone. Gap 1 only partly closed.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
finding: A small learned predictor of per-query marginal reward from extra samples lets best-of-k allocate samples by predicted difficulty. Savings are large on code and math, small on chat, and the oracle gap shows the predictor is imperfect.
numbers: Best-of-k: up to 50% less compute at equal success on Math and Code; at moderate-to-high budgets (B>=8) savings are 25-50%; gains marginal at B<8. Chat (Gemma-7b-it, LMSYS, reward model Llama-3-OffsetBias-RM-8B): full set 0-10% saving (oracle 15-25%); extreme-variance 'tranches' subset 25-40%. Routing Gemma-2B vs 7B, or plain vs value-augmented sampling: expensive option called only 50-75% of the time (25-40% fewer calls) at similar reward; sometimes routing beat the strong decoder.
quote: reduce computation by up to 50% at no cost to response quality, or improve quality by up to 10% at a fixed computational budget
limits: Math experiments assume a verifier exists. Predictor is trained on the same task distribution (needs labelled samples per domain). Oracle curve is clearly higher, so predicted difficulty keeps only part of the oracle saving; the paper gives curves, not one fraction. Small models (Gemma).
agent_relevance: Closest direct answer to gap 2: learned difficulty gives 25-50% saving on checkable tasks, near zero on chat. A cheap predictor trained on our own logs could drive the S0 gate, but expect less than Snell's 4x.

source: Manvi, Singh, Ermon (2024) Adaptive Inference-Time Compute: LLMs Can Predict if They Can Do Better, Even Mid-Generation
finding: The model itself is trained to emit one token that predicts whether restarting would give a better answer. This works as a stop and prune rule with no external reward model.
numbers: Llama 3.1 8B: AlpacaEval win rate vs GPT-4 21% to 34% with 16 samples; GSM8K 84% to 91%. Adaptive sampling reaches 74% of the 16-sample gain using 1.2 samples on average. 50-75% of samples can be pruned early with little loss.
quote: 74% of the improvement from using 16 samples can be achieved with only 1.2 samples on average
limits: Needs fine-tuning of the generator on LMSYS-based data, so not a pure scaffold method. 8B model, math plus chat. A prompt-only version with a frontier model was not tested.
agent_relevance: Shows a cheap self-predicted 'will more samples help' signal can work. For us the analogue is a prompted confidence check after the first sample; needs our own calibration test.

source: Huang, Huang, Leng, Liu, Huang (2025) Efficient Test-Time Scaling via Self-Calibration
finding: Distilling self-consistency confidence into the model gives a one-pass confidence. It is used for early stopping in best-of-N and for weighted voting, to spend fewer samples on easy questions.
numbers: Abstract: three LLMs, six datasets. Confidence-based early stopping on best-of-N lifts MathQA accuracy from 81.0 to 83.6 at a 16-response budget. Figure 1 labels show sample savings of 39.8%, 50.4% and 94.2% at different accuracy targets (read from figure text only).
quote: applying confidence-based Early Stopping to Best-of-N improves MathQA accuracy from 81.0 to 83.6 with a sample budget of 16 responses
limits: I read the abstract, intro and figure text; per-dataset tables not extracted, so only abstract-level numbers are firm. Needs a calibration training step. Raw LLM confidence is known to be overconfident.
agent_relevance: Confidence-gated adaptive N is plausible but needs calibration; a plain prompted confidence should not be trusted without a check on our items.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 as its own verifier makes iterative critique collapse. A sound external verifier gives large gains. Re-prompting with a sound verifier keeps most of the benefit even without detailed critiques.
numbers: 100 instances per domain (Table 1). Standard prompting vs LLM+LLM critique vs LLM+sound verifier: Game of 24 5% / 3% / 36-38%; Graph Coloring 16% / 2% / 37-38%; Blocksworld 40% / 55% / 60-87%; Mystery Blocksworld 4% / 0% / 8-10%. Verifier stats (Table 2): Game of 24 accuracy 87.0%, false positive rate 10.4% (320/3071), false negative rate 20.7%. A Graph Coloring row shows false negative 95.8% (113/118) and a Mystery Blocksworld row 97.09% (100/103). Table layout garbled in text extraction, so row assignment for Graph Coloring, Blocksworld and Mystery is my best reading.
quote: LLMs-as-verifiers are mostly insufficient to prevent these
limits: GPT-4 (2023-24), planning and puzzle domains, 100 instances each. Failure here is mostly false negatives (verifier rejects right answers), the other direction from the false-positive cap in K04. Reasoning-model verifiers not tested.
agent_relevance: Self-verification is domain dependent and can be worse than doing nothing. Gate any retry loop on an external check; measure our own judge false positive and false negative rates before using it as stop rule (G6).

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
finding: Individual judges and reward models are noisy with high false positive rates. A weak-supervision-weighted ensemble of them, without ground truth at test time, closes much of the gap to a reasoning model. A distilled 400M scorer keeps most of it cheaply.
numbers: Generator Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, K=100 samples, average over reasoning tasks: Weaver 87.7% vs o3-mini first sample 86.7% and GPT-4o first sample 69.0%. Majority-voting baseline about 72.7% average (row alignment in extracted table partly uncertain). Text: beats unweighted averaging of verifier scores by 17.1% and majority voting by 13.5% (Table 1). 400M cross-encoder keeps 98.7% of accuracy (98.2% in a figure caption) with 99.97% less verification compute. Plain weighted ensembles need labelled data; Weaver estimates weights without labels.
quote: suffer from high false positive rates
limits: Verifier ensemble uses up to 70B judges and reward models, so verification cost is large before distillation. Tasks are mainly math, science QA and reasoning; open-ended agent tasks not tested. Training the cross-encoder needs the generated pool.
agent_relevance: Evidence that many weak non-ground-truth verifiers can beat plain majority vote (gap 3 and partly gap 7). In a one-model scaffold, diverse prompted judges are the nearest analogue; correlated errors may limit it.

source: Jain et al. (2025) R2E-Gym: Procedural Environments and Hybrid Verifiers for Scaling Open-Weights SWE Agents
finding: On SWE-bench Verified, scaling agent rollouts helps, but execution-based verifiers (generated tests) and execution-free verifiers (trained patch scorer) each saturate near 42-43%. Combining them reaches 51%. Test-based verifiers cannot tell patches apart well.
numbers: R2E-Gym-32B pass@1 34.4%. Best@26 with hybrid verifier 51.0% (Best@16 hybrid 49.4%). Each verifier alone saturates about 42-43%. One ablation: removing trajectory components dropped Best@26 from 42.8% to 37.6%. Prior: SWE-Gym Best@16 32.0%, SWE-RL Best@500 with tests 41.0%.
quote: while each approach individually saturates around 42-43%
limits: Single benchmark of Python repos, 32B open model, trained verifier. Compute cost of 26 long agent rollouts plus verification is not normalised against one stronger model.
agent_relevance: Real agentic tasks do scale with samples, but the gain is capped by verifier quality, as with K04. Generated tests alone are weak selectors; pair with a second signal.

source: OPPO AI Agent Team (2025) Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: First systematic test-time scaling study for tool-using agents on GAIA (165 validation tasks). Best-of-N helps. Step-level search (beam, DVTS) does not. Reflecting at every step hurts. Reflecting only when a step scores badly helps.
numbers: GPT-4.1 baseline 55.76 average. BoN with list-wise merging 63.03; scoring merge 59.39; voting 56.8 (Table 3). Beam search 56.97 list-wise, 54.55 voting. BoN-wise best on Level 3. Reflection at every step 55.15 vs baseline 55.76; threshold <8 gives 53.66, <5 gives 52.12, <2 gives 56.36. List-wise verifier about 3 points above scoring (Table 4). Mixing GPT-4.1 with Claude-3.7, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-3.5, pass@4 74.55.
quote: knowing when the agent should reflect is more important than having the agent perform reflection at every step
limits: n=165, no confidence intervals; differences of 1-3 points are within noise. Single benchmark, one base model for most arms. Verifier is itself an LLM. Table columns partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 for web agents: gains are real but moderate (about 7 points), come from whole-trajectory resampling, and step-level search is not reliable. Supports triggered, not constant, reflection (S0/G12).

source: Balachandran et al. (2025) Inference-Time Scaling for Complex Tasks: Where We Stand and What Lies Ahead (Microsoft Research)
finding: Nine models, eight tasks including NP-hard, calendar planning, maze and spatial reasoning. Benefit of reasoning models and of repeated calls varies by task and shrinks as difficulty rises. More tokens do not mean more accuracy across models.
numbers: GPT-4o with 256 parallel calls: TSP easy 42% to 95%, nearly matching o1; TSP hard no significant gain. AIME 2025 best-of-n rises linearly in log(calls). Best-of-5 gives +10 to +15 points on many tasks, +15 to +25 on Maze. Same-task token gap: DeepSeek R1 uses at least 5x the tokens of Claude 3.7 Sonnet at accuracy within 3% on AIME 25. Llama 3.1 405B average 40% on AIME-style questions 1983-2024 but 1% on 2025 questions; reasoning models lose 7-30%.
quote: simply using more tokens does not necessarily translate to higher accuracy in these challenging regimes
limits: Upper bounds use perfect (ground-truth) verifiers and critics, so they show potential, not what a real selector gets. Non-math tasks are still puzzle-like with checkable answers.
agent_relevance: Gains transfer to some non-math planning tasks only if the answer is checkable and the task is not too hard. Hard instances stay hard. Supports an S0 gate that gives up or escalates rather than adding samples on hopeless items.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025, v3 Nov 2025) The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
finding: Original three-regime result on controllable puzzles with matched inference compute: plain model better at low complexity, thinking model better at medium, both collapse at high. The revised version answers critics with extra controls.
numbers: Max generation budget 64,000 tokens (Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek-R1/V3). Temperature-0 ablation on DeepSeek-R1 leaves collapse unchanged; in Blocks World temperature 0 collapses at N=4 while sampling delays it to N=30. River Crossing N=3 needs only 11 moves yet first failure move is as early as move 4. Tower of Hanoi N=10 needs 1023 moves; first failure typically about 10% into the solution; N=12 can fail before 50 moves while N=10 passes 100. On River Crossing N>=6 the authors say dynamics change (k=4).
limits: Authors' own rebuttal, not independent. Four puzzles only, complexity set by puzzle size, not a general difficulty measure. I read the paper text; nothing was re-run.
agent_relevance: The collapse is not purely a token-limit artefact: short River Crossing instances (11 moves) also fail. The low-complexity advantage of plain models is the part most relevant to the S0 gate.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking: A Comment on Shojaee et al.
finding: Argues the reported collapse is mostly an evaluation artefact: output token limits on move lists, and River Crossing instances for N>=6 with boat capacity 3 that have no solution. Asking for a generating function instead of the full move list gave high accuracy in preliminary tests.
numbers: Hanoi solution length about 10(2^N - 1) + C tokens at 10 tokens per move, giving N_max about 12-13 at a 64k output cap and about 13 at 100k. Reported Hanoi collapse before N=9 is below those limits, so the author concedes models may stop early by choice. River Crossing N>=6 with b=3 is unsolvable.
quote: experimental design limitations rather than fundamental reasoning failures
limits: Short comment, author calls experiments preliminary. First version assumed a wrong token model and was corrected after commenters. States Claude Opus co-wrote it. No systematic numbers per model. Does not address the 11-move River Crossing N=3 failures raised in d11.
agent_relevance: Fixing limits and impossible instances removes part of the high-complexity collapse, but not all. Treat the three-regime rule as a hypothesis to test on our own items, with generous output limits.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Filter or stop parallel reasoning chains using the model's own token-level confidence (bottom 10% group, tail confidence). Offline: confidence-weighted voting over the top traces. Online: stop traces when confidence drops below a threshold calibrated from 16 warm-up traces.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B (no tools) AIME 2025: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs cons@512 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%. DeepSeek-8B AIME25 82.3% to 87.4% (top 10% filter). Qwen3-32B AIME24 85.3% to 90.8%. Online token savings across model and dataset cells: roughly 19% to 59% for the conservative setting, up to 84.7% for the aggressive setting (a GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 cell at 97.9% accuracy; model assignment of table blocks is my reading).
quote: reduces generated tokens by up to 84.7% compared to full parallel thinking
limits: Open reasoning models only (Qwen3, DeepSeek-8B, GPT-OSS). Authors note aggressive filtering can hurt through overconfidence on wrong answers (seen on GPT-OSS-120B) and suggest the conservative setting. Baseline is 512 full traces, a very expensive baseline, so savings are relative to a large N. Some head-based filters in the appendix were no better than plain majority vote.
agent_relevance: Strong candidate stop-and-filter rule for parallel chains (gap 6) and a no-verifier selector. Needs token log-probs, which a hosted API agent may not expose.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: At 'Wait'-style transition points, the model writes a trial answer; if its confidence in that answer is high, generation stops. Training-free.
numbers: 11 reasoning LLMs, 10 benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC, GPQA, AIME, LiveCodeBench): chain-of-thought length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average while accuracy changes by +0.3% to +5.0%.
quote: reducing the length of CoT sequences by an average of 19.1% to 80.1% while improving accuracy by 0.3% to 5.0%
limits: Range is across models and benchmarks, not a single figure. Needs access to token probabilities of the trial answer. Single-chain method; combination with parallel voting not tested here. I read the abstract and intro, not every table.
agent_relevance: Confidence exit on a trial answer is a cheap S0/stop rule for one chain. Combine only after testing, since overconfidence is the known failure.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Reasoning models usually reach their final answer well before the end. Three stop rules: stop when the answer repeats, boost the end-of-thinking token probability, or a probe on internal activations.
numbers: Models converge after about 60% of reasoning steps on math. Five benchmarks, five open-weight LLMs. On NaturalQuestions, answer-consistency stopping cuts tokens by over 40% and slightly raises accuracy.
quote: models typically converge to their final answers after 60% of the reasoning steps
limits: Open-weight models only. The limitations section lists combining answer stability with other signals as future work, so the combination question (gap 6) is open. Activation probe needs model access. I read abstract and limitations, not every table.
agent_relevance: Cheap external rule that needs no logits: re-ask the interim answer and stop when it repeats k times. Testable in our scaffold.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR Dec 2025)
finding: Designed tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy. Five failure modes: Claude gets more distracted by irrelevant facts; o-series resist distractors but overfit to problem framing; drift from sensible priors to spurious features; poor focus on long deduction; more self-preservation talk in Claude Sonnet 4 on a safety task.
numbers: Misleading Math/Python counting tasks with 1 to 5 distractors, 500 questions per distractor count. Claude Opus 4 accuracy falls from nearly 100% as reasoning grows (controlled and natural setups). DeepSeek R1 natural overthinking: 70% to 30% with five distractors. o3 mostly stable on distractors. Regression with spurious features: few-shot examples largely corrected the drift. Controlled setup: budgets 0 to 16384 tokens requested; natural setup: 5 samples ranked by their own length.
quote: Claude models become increasingly distracted by irrelevant information
limits: Tasks were built to expose the effect, so it shows existence, not frequency. Natural-setup length ranking is correlational. Mitigations tested are limited: few-shot examples for the spurious-feature mode; no test of a distractor filter or a hard budget cap as a fix.
agent_relevance: Failure modes 1, 3 and 4 map to our scaffold: long scratchpads with distracting memory, framing bias, and long constraint tracking. Worth a regression test with distractors injected into memory; a cap alone is untested.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Let the model pre-think about a stored context before any question arrives, then answer questions from the processed context. It cuts test-time tokens and the effect grows when queries are predictable from the context and when many questions share one context.
numbers: Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME: about 5x less test-time compute at equal accuracy (o1 showed limited gain). More sleep-time compute: up to +13% (GSM-Symbolic) and +18% (AIME). Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: average cost per query down 2.5x when amortised over related queries; with 2 questions per context sleep-time compute is less favourable, with 10 per context it improves the cost-accuracy frontier. Gain rises with a query-predictability score. Agentic SWE-Features case: sleep-time better at low test budgets, plain test-time better at higher budgets. 5 parallel sleep generations usually beat 10.
quote: sleep-time compute is most beneficial in settings where the question can be predicted from the context
limits: Tasks were rewritten so that context and question are separable, which favours the method. At high test budgets plain test-time compute wins (authors suggest less distracting content). Predictability was measured by a small LM score.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to the memory part: precompute summaries and derived facts for contexts reused across many questions (about 10 or more), not for one-off questions. Expect no gain when queries are unpredictable.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without external feedback, asking the same model to review and revise its answer does not help and often hurts. At matched response counts, self-consistency does better than self-correction or multi-agent debate.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 (standard) to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. Table 7 (GSM8K): single response 76.7; self-consistency 82.5, 85.3, 88.2 at 3, 6, 9 responses; debate numbers are 83.2 and 83.0 but I could not align them to rounds from the extracted text. With oracle labels telling when to stop, self-correction looks good, which is the flaw in earlier reports.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4), 1-2 correction rounds, three datasets. Reasoning models trained for self-verification may behave differently; d02 shows refinement can win at matched tokens when chains see prior attempts and are short.
agent_relevance: Support for gating revision loops on an external signal and comparing them to plain resampling at equal calls before keeping them (G6/G12).
